Lead case study

Do star ratings actually match what people write?

331,226 Google Play reviews across 28 entertainment apps, tested for the gap between what people click and what they type.

Negative61.3%
Positive28.1%
Neutral10.6%

Sentiment class distribution, 331,226 reviews

The dataset skewed 61.3% negative - the opposite of the starting hypothesis. Logistic Regression beat Naive Bayes on macro F1 (0.642 vs. 0.535) because Naive Bayes barely predicted the Neutral class at all.

The real story isn't "3-star reviews are ambiguous." It's that the model over-predicts Neutral for reviews that are actually Negative - 48.19% of every mismatch follows that one pattern.

How I work

The approach behind every case

01

Let the metric decide

Accuracy looks fine right up until one class gets ignored. I pick the metric that can't be fooled by an imbalanced dataset, then let it choose the model - not the other way around.

02

Check the data from every angle

A category can look weak on one metric and strong on another. I slice by category, geography, and time before deciding what the pattern actually is.

03

Say what I'd do differently

Every case here includes what I'd change next time - a missed availability check, an untested bundling assumption. Evidence over decoration applies to my own process too.

Case Study 01 · NLP · Classification

Sentiment Analysis of 28 Entertainment Apps

Do star ratings actually match what people write? Tested across 336,000 scraped reviews, narrowed to 331,226 after cleaning.

331,226
reviews analyzed
28
apps, 12k reviews each
0.642
macro F1, Logistic Regression
28.12%
star/text mismatch rate
View the project
The problem Method & decisions What came of it The evidence What I'd do differently
The problem

A 4-star review that reads like a complaint

While using the Play Store, I kept running into reviews like "good app but keeps crashing every hour, this annoys me" - a decent star rating sitting next to frustrated text. Or a low star next to a review that read more like a pricing complaint than actual dislike for the app.

That made me ask a plain question: does the star rating actually match what people write? I set out to test it across 28 entertainment apps - 12,000 reviews scraped per app, 336,000 total, narrowing to 331,226 English-language reviews after cleaning.

Method & decisions

Letting the numbers pick the model

01

Model comparison, not model preference

Tested Logistic Regression against Naive Bayes and let macro F1 - not raw accuracy - decide the winner. Naive Bayes had higher accuracy but barely predicted the Neutral class at all, which macro F1 catches and accuracy hides.

02

Kept negation words on purpose

Stripping words like "not" from the vocabulary would let the model misread negated phrases and flip a prediction the wrong way.

03

Added bigrams to close the gap

"not" and "good" as two separate features still don't tell the model "not good" is negative. Treating "not_good" as one feature does - and it produced a measured gain, not just a hoped-for one.

04

Built my own check on my own findings

Compared the star-based label against the ML-based label directly, specifically to test whether the result was worth trusting before reporting it.

05

Balanced the sample before topic modeling

Made sure every app had the same number of reviews before running LDA - comparing apps unevenly would have made any pattern look unfair, and LDA needs enough sample size per group to be reliable.

What came of it

The dataset skewed negative - and the mismatch wasn't where I expected

The dataset skewed negative: 61.3% Negative, 28.1% Positive, 10.6% Neutral - overturning the hypothesis that it would be mostly positive. Logistic Regression won on macro F1 (0.642 vs. 0.535), even though Naive Bayes had higher raw accuracy, because Naive Bayes rarely predicted Neutral correctly.

The most interesting result wasn't the one I expected going in. The ambiguity wasn't really about 3-star reviews being unstable - it was the model's decision-making. It fell back on the Neutral label far more often than the actual share of Neutral reviews justified, even when the true rating was clearly Negative. That's why the single biggest mismatch pattern is Negative-rated reviews reading as Neutral to the model - not Positive-rated reviews hiding negativity, which is what I'd originally assumed.

"28.12% of reviews disagree with their own star rating. The biggest gap isn't where I expected it to be."

The evidence

Class distribution and the failure mode

Fig. 1 - Sentiment class distribution across 331,226 reviews, pulled directly from the notebook
Fig. 2 - Confusion matrix, Logistic Regression. 8,979 Negative reviews (22.1% of all Negatives) predicted as Neutral - the largest single error cell on the matrix, and the direct evidence for the "model over-predicts Neutral" finding
What I'd do differently

Check availability before running the full pipeline

I started with 48 apps. Only after scraping all of them did I find a chunk came back with zero reviews - dead links, bad package IDs, apps that had changed. Rerunning the whole pipeline at that point was already time-consuming, so I cut down to the 28 apps that had full data instead of scraping again.

Next time, I'd check review availability per app before running the full pipeline - that way I catch the gap without burning a full run to find it.

Case Study 02 · Power BI · Business Analytics

AdventureWorks - Power BI Dashboards

Bikes drove almost all the revenue. Accessories drove almost all the margin. The dashboard exists to make both true statements visible at once.

Bikes revenue
$0.7M
Accessories revenue

Accessories margin
43.24%
Bikes margin
View the project
The problem Method & decisions What came of it The evidence What I'd do differently
The problem

A revenue gap that doesn't tell the whole story

Working through the AdventureWorks dataset, I noticed something worth digging into: Bikes generated $28.3M in revenue and $11.5M in profit, while Accessories brought in only $0.7M in revenue and $438.6K in profit - even though Accessories actually had more orders (18K vs. 15K) and a better profit margin percentage (62.60% vs. 43.24%).

Method & decisions

Slicing the data before deciding anything

01

Built the full dashboard set

Revenue, profit, margin, and order counts, sliced by category, country, and year - to see the full picture before drawing a conclusion from any single number.

02

Looked at every angle before recommending anything

A category can look weak on one metric (total revenue) while actually being strong on another (margin, order count) - the dashboard needed to hold both at once.

03

Turned the pattern into a decision

Based on the revenue-vs-margin split, the recommendation is to bundle Bikes and Accessories at point of sale - so a margin-strong category stops relying on being bought alone.

What came of it

Two categories, two different kinds of strong

Bikes drove the overwhelming majority of revenue and profit. Accessories lagged far behind in raw revenue despite higher order volume and a materially better margin. This is what actually clicked working through the dataset: understanding how revenue, profit, and margin relate to each other, and how a category can look weak on one metric while being strong on another.

The evidence

Revenue vs. margin, side by side

Fig. 1 - Sales Overview page. Bikes at $28.3M dwarfs Accessories at $0.7M in the "Total Revenue by Category" panel - the number that opens the case, not decoration
Fig. 2 - Product Analysis page. "Profit Margin % by Category" is the exact evidence for the bundling recommendation: Accessories 62.60% vs. Bikes 43.24% vs. Clothing 38.10%
What I'd do differently

Test the bundling idea with data, not just propose it

Next time, I'd build a second, comparison-focused dashboard - specifically a view showing what percentage of bike buyers also bought an accessory in the same transaction - to actually test the bundling recommendation with data instead of just proposing it.

Case Study 03 · Excel · Market Research

Data Analyst Job Market Research - Pakistan vs. Global

Most curricula weight Python heavily. Twenty real job descriptions say otherwise.

11/20

View the project
The problem Method & decisions What came of it The evidence What I'd do differently
The problem

What curricula teach vs. what employers ask for

Most institutes teaching data analytics focus heavily on Python. But from what I'd read and heard, SQL and other skills like Excel - along with soft skills like communication - needed to be just as strong. So I collected 20 real job descriptions, 10 from Pakistani companies and 10 from foreign companies, and built a dataset around them to see what employers were actually asking for, technically and beyond.

Method & decisions

AI-assisted extraction, manually validated

01

Extracted with AI, validated by hand

Used AI to pull required technical skills, tools, soft skills, and experience requirements from each job description, then validated that extraction myself before building the dashboard.

02

Built the frequency dataset

Organized the extracted data into an Excel dashboard - the hardest part was pulling consistent signal out of long, differently-structured job descriptions.

What came of it

SQL leads, Python trails, communication tops the soft skills

The results confirmed the pattern I suspected: SQL appeared in 16 of 20 JDs, the single most demanded skill, followed by Power BI (10/20 as a skill, 12/20 as a tool) and Excel (6/20 as a skill, 11/20 as a tool). Python appeared in only 2 of 20 - it still matters, especially in emerging and senior roles, but in this sample it came up far less than curriculum weight would suggest. Communication was the top soft skill, appearing in 11 of 20 JDs.

It told me what I actually needed to learn as a data analytics student, based on what the real world demands - not just what's taught in class.

The evidence

Skill frequency across 20 job descriptions

Fig. 1 - The 6-chart Excel dashboard built from all 20 job descriptions. SQL and Power BI lead the technical-skill frequency count; Communication leads the soft-skills donut

Fig. 2 - Skill frequency, simplified: SQL and communication outrank Python by a wide margin
What I'd do differently

Target senior roles, hold off on Power BI

Next time, I'd collect more JDs and specifically target senior-level postings to see if Python's importance grows there - even though gathering more data is time-consuming. I'd keep using Excel for a dataset this size, and only move to Power BI if working with a much larger dataset (20,000+ records).
